newsitem.title: INDIA: India not "unduly alarmed" over import curbs.
newsitem.headline: India not "unduly alarmed" over import curbs.

text.p: India is not unduly alarmed by some of its trading partners starting a case in the World Trade Organisation (WTO) against its import curbs, Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah was quoted as saying on Thursday.
The Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted Ramaiah as saying India was confident of resolving the issue amicably. "Nothing is going to happen. We can handle the situation," Ramaiah added.
The European Union said on Thursday it would join other trade powers in starting a case in the WTO against India's decades-old import restrictions.

The move follows a similar decision earlier in the week by the United States, which has since been followed by Canada, Australia and New Zealand, all of whom argue the Indian measures run against WTO open trading accords.

PTI quoted Ramaiah as saying India had already reduced the timeframe for removing quantitative restrictions on imports to six years from an earlier proposal for nine years, and would stick to the six-year period.
"Many countries, particularly in the European Union, are sympathetic towards us and will support us," he said without elaborating.
"We have also made substantial modifications on easing imports along 2,700 commodity tariff lines after discussing it with various countries," Ramaiah told PTI.
Ramaiah said he would take up the issue with Australia when Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer visited India on July 22.
Fischer said on Wednesday that although the restrictions denied his country's exporters fair access to the Indian market, he hoped for an early settlement through consultations.
Ramaiah said India would also be able to win over the United States to its point of view.

The restrictions, which affect some 2,700 items ranging from consumer goods to agricultural products, have been in force since the 1950s, but were accepted by other countries because of India's earlier endemic balance-of-payments problems.
But with the steady growth in the country's foreign exchange reserves, which reached $28.8 billion in June, other WTO members have insisted that Delhi agree to move quickly to drop the curbs.

The United States was reported pressing for a maximum of three years, while the EU and other WTO members were indicating readiness to accept five years if restrictions on most big-ticket items were removed early in the period.

A Commerce Ministry spokeswoman confirmed the PTI report was correct but declined further comment. Analysts in Delhi said earlier this month it was likely that India would now propose a five-year phase-out of restrictions.
Under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, India has to respond to the requests for consultations within 10 days and start them within 20 days.

If after two months no solution is in sight, the complaining powers can ask the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body to set up a panel to rule on the issue. But some have said they would not like the problem to go that far.
